dx: Chronic aortic regurgitation from aortic root dilation
case: A 34-year-old man comes to the physician because of fatigue and a pounding sensation in his chest when he lies on his left side. He is 196 cm tall, and his arm span exceeds his height. Ophthalmologic examination 1 year ago showed bilateral upward subluxation of the lenses. His father died suddenly of an aortic dissection at age 41 years. Blood pressure is 152/48 mm Hg, and peripheral pulses are bounding. A high-pitched, early diastolic decrescendo murmur is heard best with the patient sitting up and leaning forward at end-expiration. Echocardiography shows an aortic root diameter of 5.1 cm (reference under about 4.0 cm), moderate to severe aortic regurgitation, and a dilated left ventricle with an ejection fraction of 58% (reference 55% to 70%). Diagnosis: chronic aortic regurgitation due to aortic root dilation.

questions.stem: Genetic testing in this patient is most likely to show a mutation in the gene encoding which of the following proteins?
options: Type III collagen, a fibrillar collagen of vessel walls
Cystathionine beta-synthase, an enzyme of homocysteine use
Fibrillin-1, a glycoprotein of elastic fiber microfibrils
Elastin, the core protein of arterial elastic lamellae
approach: Group the clues: tall build, long arm span, upward lens displacement, aortic root dilation, father with dissection.
Recognize Marfan syndrome, autosomal dominant.
Recall the gene: FBN1 on chromosome 15, which encodes fibrillin-1.
questions.why: This is Marfan syndrome. FBN1 encodes fibrillin-1, which forms the microfibril scaffold that elastic fibers are built on. Defective fibrillin-1 weakens the aortic media (cystic medial degeneration) and the suspensory ligaments of the lens. Fibrillin-1 also normally holds TGF-beta in an inactive form, so loss of it increases TGF-beta signaling, which adds to aortic root enlargement.
whyNot: Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (COL3A1) causes arterial and bowel rupture with thin, translucent skin. It does not cause tall stature or lens dislocation.
Homocystinuria (CBS deficiency) can give a tall build and lens dislocation, but the lenses usually shift downward, inheritance is autosomal recessive, and the main vascular problem is thrombosis.
Correct.
Elastin (ELN) loss in Williams syndrome causes supravalvular aortic stenosis, not root dilation with lens displacement.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in his left ventricular pressure-volume loop, compared with a normal loop, is most likely in this chronic, compensated state?
options: Larger end-diastolic volume and stroke volume, with a higher peak systolic pressure
Normal end-diastolic volume and smaller stroke volume, with a much higher peak systolic pressure
Larger end-diastolic and end-systolic volumes, with a smaller stroke volume
Smaller end-diastolic volume and smaller stroke volume, with a normal peak pressure
approach: Identify the lesion: wide pulse pressure and early diastolic decrescendo murmur mean aortic regurgitation.
Ask which phase is lost: the leaky aortic valve lets blood enter the ventricle from the aorta as soon as ejection ends.
Add the volume load: regurgitant blood plus normal atrial filling raises end-diastolic volume and total stroke volume.
questions.why: In aortic regurgitation, blood flows back into the left ventricle from the aorta during diastole, so the ventricle starts filling the moment ejection stops. Because the ventricle is never a closed chamber at that point, there is no true isovolumetric relaxation. The regurgitant volume adds to normal filling from the atrium, so end-diastolic volume rises, and the Frank-Starling mechanism produces a large total stroke volume. That large stroke volume raises systolic pressure, and the back-leak lowers diastolic pressure, which explains the 152/48 reading.
whyNot: Correct.
This is aortic stenosis: the ventricle must generate a much higher systolic pressure to push blood through a narrow valve, while stroke volume does not rise.
This is systolic heart failure, as in dilated cardiomyopathy. His ejection fraction of 58% shows that contraction is still preserved.
This is mitral stenosis: a narrow mitral valve limits filling, so end-diastolic volume and stroke volume both fall.

questions.stem: His murmur is produced by blood flowing across one valve during part of the cardiac cycle. Which of the following best describes when this flow begins?
options: At S1, when left ventricular pressure rises above left atrial pressure
After an opening snap, when left atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure
After an ejection click, when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure
At A2, when left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure
approach: Place the murmur in the cycle: early diastolic and decrescendo.
Name the valve: the aortic valve should be closed during diastole.
Link it to pressures: once ejection ends, aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, and a leaky aortic valve lets blood flow back.
questions.why: At the end of ejection, left ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure and the aortic valve closes, producing A2. In aortic regurgitation the cusps do not seal, so blood flows back from the high-pressure aorta into the relaxing ventricle starting at that moment. The gradient is largest early in diastole and narrows as the ventricle fills and aortic pressure falls, which is why the murmur is decrescendo.
whyNot: This describes mitral regurgitation, a holosystolic murmur that starts with S1 and is heard best at the apex.
This describes mitral stenosis, a low-pitched diastolic rumble that starts after the opening snap of a stiff mitral valve.
This describes forward flow through a stenotic aortic valve (often a bicuspid valve with an ejection click), which produces a systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur.
Correct.

topics: Timing of murmurs in the cardiac cycle

questions.stem: His ventricle has handled the extra volume for years with a near-normal ejection fraction. Which of the following structural adaptations of the left ventricle best explains this?
options: Concentric hypertrophy, with new sarcomeres added in parallel
Eccentric hypertrophy, with new sarcomeres added in series
Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with myocyte disarray
Interstitial amyloid deposition with a stiff, thick wall
approach: Identify the load: aortic regurgitation causes volume overload.
Match load to remodeling: volume overload leads to eccentric hypertrophy, pressure overload leads to concentric hypertrophy.
Link structure to function: a larger cavity can eject a larger stroke volume at the same ejection fraction.
questions.why: Chronic aortic regurgitation is a volume overload. Myocytes respond by adding sarcomeres in series, so the cells lengthen and the chamber enlarges, with a modest increase in wall thickness. The larger chamber holds the extra volume at a tolerable filling pressure and ejects a large stroke volume, so forward output is maintained for years. Over time, rising wall stress and fibrosis lead to systolic dysfunction and heart failure.
whyNot: Concentric hypertrophy is the response to pressure overload, as in aortic stenosis or systemic hypertension. Wall thickness rises while the cavity stays normal or small.
Correct.
This is hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a genetic sarcomere disease, not an adaptation to valve leakage.
Amyloid infiltration causes restrictive cardiomyopathy with a stiff, non-dilated ventricle.

topics: Ventricular remodeling: volume versus pressure overload

case: A 29-year-old woman, gravida 1, para 0, at 26 weeks' gestation comes to the physician because of worsening shortness of breath, two-pillow orthopnea, and cough with blood-streaked sputum. She grew up in a rural area with limited access to medical care. At age 10 years, she had an illness with fever and painful, swollen knees and ankles. Pulse is 108/min and regular. Cardiac examination shows a loud S1, an opening snap after S2, and a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex. Echocardiography shows thickened mitral leaflets with commissural fusion, a mitral valve area of 1.1 cm2 (reference 4 to 6 cm2), and an enlarged left atrium. Diagnosis: rheumatic mitral stenosis.

questions.stem: The valve damage began years ago after a streptococcal pharyngitis. Which immune mechanism best explains how that infection injured her heart?
options: Type I hypersensitivity, with IgE-armed mast cells degranulating in the valve
Type II hypersensitivity, with antibodies that cross-react with heart proteins
Type III hypersensitivity, with immune complexes trapped in valve capillaries
Persistent bacterial infection of the valve leaflets with local complement activation
approach: Link the history: fever and migrating large-joint arthritis in childhood suggest acute rheumatic fever.
Recall the cause: group A streptococcal pharyngitis followed by an immune reaction, not direct infection.
Classify it: antibodies against streptococcal antigens (M protein) bind similar host proteins, which is molecular mimicry and type II hypersensitivity.
questions.why: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal pharyngitis by about 2 to 4 weeks. Antibodies made against streptococcal antigens, especially M protein, cross-react with host proteins in the heart such as cardiac myosin and valve components. This is molecular mimicry, classified as type II hypersensitivity, and T cells reacting to the same shared antigens add to the damage. Repeated inflammation heals by fibrosis, producing thickened leaflets with commissural fusion years later.
whyNot: Type I reactions cause allergy and anaphylaxis within minutes of antigen exposure. They do not cause delayed valve scarring.
Correct.
Immune complex deposition is the mechanism of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis, which follows the same organism but affects the kidney.
Rheumatic fever is a sterile, immune-mediated disease. Live bacteria growing on a valve describes infective endocarditis.

questions.stem: Before pregnancy, her resting pulse was 72/min and she had no symptoms. It is now 108/min. Which of the following best explains how this change in heart rate produced her symptoms?
options: A faster rate increases backflow from the ventricle into the left atrium in systole
A faster rate weakens ventricular contraction and lowers forward stroke volume
A shorter systole raises aortic pressure and the afterload on the left ventricle
A shorter diastole raises the left atrial pressure needed to fill the ventricle
approach: Identify the lesion: a narrow mitral valve limits flow from the left atrium to the left ventricle.
Recall that tachycardia shortens diastole much more than systole.
Apply it: the same filling volume must cross the valve in less time, so the pressure gradient and left atrial pressure rise and back up into the lungs.
questions.why: Flow across a stenotic mitral valve happens only in diastole and depends on the pressure gradient and the time available. As heart rate rises, diastole shortens much more than systole. To fill the ventricle in less time, the gradient across the valve must rise, so left atrial pressure climbs. That pressure passes back to the pulmonary veins and capillaries, causing dyspnea, orthopnea, and blood-streaked sputum. This is why pregnancy, fever, exercise, and atrial fibrillation with a fast rate often unmask mitral stenosis.
whyNot: Systolic backflow is mitral regurgitation. In pure mitral stenosis the valve closes, so there is no systolic leak to increase.
Healthy myocardium contracts more strongly at faster rates (the force-frequency effect), and in mitral stenosis the left ventricle itself is normal. The problem is filling.
Heart rate does not raise afterload in this way, and afterload is not the limiting step in mitral stenosis.
Correct.

topics: Diastolic filling time and heart rate

questions.stem: Months later she develops atrial fibrillation, and transesophageal echocardiography shows a thrombus in the left atrial appendage. This part of the left atrium develops from which embryonic structure?
options: Primitive atrium
Common pulmonary vein
Right horn of the sinus venosus
Septum primum
approach: Recognize the typical site of thrombus in atrial fibrillation: the left atrial appendage.
Recall the two embryonic sources of the adult left atrium.
Match them: trabeculated appendage from the primitive atrium, smooth-walled part from the pulmonary veins.
questions.why: The adult left atrium has two embryonic sources. The smooth-walled main portion forms when the common pulmonary vein and its branches are absorbed into the atrial wall. The original primitive atrium is left behind as the trabeculated, pouch-like appendage. Blood stagnates in this narrow, ridged pouch when the atrium no longer contracts, so it is the usual site of thrombus in atrial fibrillation and mitral stenosis.
whyNot: Correct.
The common pulmonary vein is absorbed into the left atrial wall to form its smooth-walled main part, not the trabeculated appendage.
The right sinus horn forms the smooth-walled part of the right atrium (sinus venarum), not any part of the left atrium.
The septum primum forms part of the interatrial septum (including the flap of the foramen ovale), not the appendage.

questions.stem: Her sputum contains macrophages filled with golden-brown granules that stain blue with Prussian blue. Which process best explains these cells?
options: Peroxidation of organelle membranes inside the macrophages, leaving lipofuscin granules
Inhaled carbon particles from air pollution taken up by alveolar macrophages
Small bleeds from congested alveolar capillaries, with hemoglobin stored as hemosiderin
Bilirubin crystals formed in macrophages from hemolysis within the circulation
approach: Read the stain: Prussian blue positive means iron, which in tissue is hemosiderin.
Ask where the iron came from: red cells that leaked into alveoli.
Link to the lesion: mitral stenosis raises left atrial and pulmonary capillary pressure, causing chronic passive congestion and small bleeds.
questions.why: In mitral stenosis, high left atrial pressure passes back to the pulmonary veins and capillaries, causing chronic passive congestion. Engorged capillaries leak red cells into the alveoli. Alveolar macrophages engulf these red cells and break hemoglobin down, storing the iron as hemosiderin, which is golden-brown and Prussian blue positive. These hemosiderin-laden macrophages are often called heart failure cells, and the same small bleeds explain her blood-streaked sputum.
whyNot: Lipofuscin is a wear-and-tear pigment of aging cells. It is yellow-brown but does not stain with Prussian blue because it holds no iron.
Anthracotic pigment is black and does not contain iron, so it does not stain with Prussian blue.
Correct.
Bilirubin does not contain iron, so it is Prussian blue negative, and intravascular hemolysis does not load alveolar macrophages with pigment.

topics: Chronic passive congestion of the lung

case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician because of brief episodes of palpitations and occasional sharp chest pain unrelated to exertion. Pulse is 74/min, and blood pressure is 112/70 mm Hg. Auscultation at the apex shows a midsystolic click followed by a short, late systolic murmur. She does not have tall stature, lens subluxation, or joint hypermobility. Echocardiography shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets, with the posterior leaflet billowing more than 2 mm above the annulus into the left atrium during systole, and mild mitral regurgitation. Ejection fraction is 63% (reference 55% to 70%). Diagnosis: mitral valve prolapse.

questions.stem: She is examined while squatting and again immediately after she stands up. Which of the following changes in her auscultatory findings is most likely on standing?
options: Later click and shorter murmur, because left ventricular end-diastolic volume falls
Later click and shorter murmur, because left ventricular end-diastolic volume rises
Earlier click and longer murmur, because left ventricular end-diastolic volume rises
Earlier click and longer murmur, because left ventricular end-diastolic volume falls
approach: Recall what standing does: blood pools in the legs, venous return and preload fall.
Link volume to prolapse: a smaller ventricle leaves the redundant leaflet and chordae relatively longer, so the leaflet prolapses earlier in systole.
Predict: earlier click, longer murmur.
questions.why: Standing suddenly reduces venous return, so left ventricular end-diastolic volume falls. In a smaller ventricle the redundant leaflet and its chordae are relatively too long for the chamber, so the leaflet reaches its prolapse point earlier in systole. The click moves closer to S1 and the late systolic murmur lengthens. Squatting, which raises venous return and afterload, does the reverse. Valsalva strain acts like standing.
whyNot: Smaller volume makes the prolapse happen sooner, so the click moves earlier, not later.
This is the effect of squatting: more venous return and higher afterload enlarge the ventricle, so the click moves later. Standing does the opposite.
Standing lowers venous return, so ventricular volume falls rather than rises.
Correct.

questions.stem: The midsystolic click is produced when the prolapsing leaflet is suddenly checked during ventricular contraction. Sudden tensing of which structure produces the click?
options: Septomarginal trabecula
Chordae tendineae
Pectinate muscles
Crista terminalis
approach: Recall how the mitral valve is held shut in systole: papillary muscles contract and pull on chordae tendineae.
Apply it to prolapse: the redundant leaflet balloons back until its chordae snap taut.
Choose the structure that tenses at that moment.
questions.why: During ventricular systole the papillary muscles contract and their chordae tendineae hold the mitral leaflets so they meet without everting into the left atrium. In mitral valve prolapse the leaflets and chordae are redundant, so the leaflet billows backward until the slack chordae suddenly tighten. That sudden tensing produces the midsystolic click. The murmur that follows is the mitral regurgitation that starts once the leaflets no longer meet.
whyNot: The septomarginal trabecula (moderator band) is in the right ventricle and carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle. It is not attached to the mitral valve.
Correct.
Pectinate muscles are ridges in the atrial walls and appendages. They do not connect to the valve leaflets.
The crista terminalis is a ridge in the right atrium between its smooth and trabeculated parts, unrelated to the mitral valve.

questions.stem: A resected leaflet from a patient with the same disease shows a markedly expanded middle (spongiosa) layer. The material that expands this layer and draws water into it is best described as which of the following?
options: Amyloid fibrils with a beta-pleated sheet structure
Hydroxyapatite crystals of calcium phosphate
Proteoglycans with glycosaminoglycan side chains
Cholesterol esters stored within foam cells
approach: Recall the histology of mitral valve prolapse: myxomatous degeneration of the spongiosa.
Ask which matrix molecules hold water: glycosaminoglycans are highly negatively charged and attract water.
Pick proteoglycans, the core-protein molecules that carry glycosaminoglycan chains.
questions.why: Mitral valve prolapse is caused by myxomatous degeneration. The spongiosa layer fills with proteoglycans, whose glycosaminoglycan side chains (such as chondroitin sulfate and dermatan sulfate) carry many negative charges and bind water. At the same time collagen and elastic fibers in the fibrosa become fragmented. The leaflets become thick, soft, and redundant, so they balloon into the atrium under systolic pressure.
whyNot: Amyloid is a misfolded protein deposit that stiffens tissue. It is seen in restrictive cardiomyopathy, not floppy leaflets.
Calcium phosphate deposits make valve cusps rigid, as in calcific aortic stenosis.
Correct.
Lipid-laden foam cells are a feature of atherosclerotic plaques.

questions.stem: Six years later she has had fever up to 38.4 °C (101.1 °F) and fatigue for three weeks. The fever began about two weeks after a tooth extraction. Blood cultures grow alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant, gram-positive cocci in chains. Which property of this organism best explains how it settles on her mitral valve?
options: Dextran that binds fibrin-platelet deposits on the damaged leaflet
M protein that blocks complement deposition and neutrophil phagocytosis
Coagulase that converts fibrinogen to fibrin around the bacteria
IgA protease that cleaves secretory antibody at mucosal surfaces
approach: Identify the organism: alpha-hemolytic, optochin-resistant streptococci after dental work are viridans group streptococci.
Recall the setting: subacute endocarditis on a previously abnormal valve.
Link virulence to site: dextran lets the bacteria stick to fibrin-platelet deposits on the damaged leaflet.
questions.why: Viridans group streptococci live in the mouth and enter the blood during dental procedures. An abnormal, regurgitant valve develops small sterile fibrin-platelet deposits where flow is turbulent. Strains such as Streptococcus sanguinis make dextran, an extracellular polysaccharide that binds these fibrin-platelet deposits, so the bacteria adhere and grow into vegetations. The course is subacute, with weeks of low-grade fever and fatigue.
whyNot: Correct.
M protein is the main virulence factor of group A streptococci, which are beta-hemolytic and rarely cause endocarditis.
Coagulase is the marker of Staphylococcus aureus, a gram-positive coccus in clusters that causes acute endocarditis, often on normal valves.
IgA protease helps Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria, and Haemophilus colonize mucosa. Pneumococci are optochin sensitive.

dx: Chronic rheumatic heart disease with mitral stenosis and aortic regurgitation
case: A 52-year-old man is referred to a cardiac surgeon because of worsening exertional dyspnea and ankle swelling. He had acute rheumatic fever at age 9 years and a recurrence at age 14 years after another episode of pharyngitis. Pulse is 84/min and irregularly irregular. Cardiac examination shows a low-pitched diastolic rumble at the apex, a soft early diastolic decrescendo murmur at the left sternal border, a loud P2, and a left parasternal heave. Echocardiography shows thickened, restricted mitral leaflets with a valve area of 1.3 cm2 (reference 4 to 6 cm2), mild aortic regurgitation, right ventricular hypertrophy, and an estimated pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 58 mm Hg (reference 15 to 30 mm Hg). Diagnosis: chronic rheumatic heart disease.

questions.stem: He undergoes mitral valve replacement. Which of the following gross findings is most likely in the excised mitral valve?
options: Thick leaflets, fused commissures, and short, thick, fused chordae
Bulky, friable vegetations that have eroded through the leaflets
Thin, ballooning leaflets with long, thin, stretched chordae
Calcium nodules at the leaflet bases with free, unfused commissures
approach: Recall that chronic rheumatic disease follows repeated inflammation that heals by fibrosis.
Picture where scarring occurs: leaflet edges and commissures fuse, and chordae shorten and fuse.
Match the gross picture: a narrow, fish-mouth orifice.
questions.why: Chronic rheumatic heart disease is the scarred end stage of repeated bouts of valvulitis. Fibrosis thickens the leaflets, fuses them at the commissures, and shortens, thickens, and fuses the chordae tendineae. The result is a rigid, funnel-shaped mitral orifice often called a fish-mouth or buttonhole deformity. The mitral valve is involved most often, followed by the aortic valve, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.
Destructive vegetations are typical of acute infective endocarditis, often caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
Ballooning leaflets with elongated chordae describe myxomatous mitral valve prolapse.
Calcium at the base with free commissures describes degenerative calcification, such as mitral annular calcification or calcific aortic stenosis.

topics: Gross pathology of rheumatic valve disease

questions.stem: His second attack at 14 followed a new streptococcal pharyngitis and added to the damage from the first. Which feature of adaptive immunity best explains why a later infection can quickly re-trigger the cross-reactive response?
options: Plasma cells switch from IgG back to IgM production to respond faster on re-exposure
Natural killer cells recognize streptococcal peptides presented on MHC class I
Memory B and T cells formed in the first attack respond rapidly on re-exposure
Mast cells coated with IgE in the first attack degranulate on re-exposure
approach: Recall that rheumatic fever is an adaptive, antigen-specific response that cross-reacts with heart proteins.
Apply the principle of immunologic memory: the first response leaves memory B and T cells.
On a new infection those cells respond faster and more strongly, so recurrences add cumulative damage.
questions.why: The first episode of rheumatic fever creates long-lived memory B and T cells specific for streptococcal antigens that also cross-react with heart proteins. A later group A streptococcal pharyngitis reactivates these cells, so the secondary response is faster and larger. Each recurrence adds new valve inflammation, and the scarring is cumulative. This is why patients with a history of rheumatic fever are given long-term antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent new streptococcal infections.
whyNot: Class switching goes from IgM to IgG, IgA, or IgE and cannot be reversed. A secondary response is mainly IgG.
Natural killer cells do not recognize specific peptides on MHC class I. They kill cells that have lost MHC class I or show stress signals.
Correct.
IgE-coated mast cells mediate type I hypersensitivity, which is not the mechanism of rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: A throat culture from his original pharyngitis would most likely have shown which laboratory profile?
options: Beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-resistant, CAMP-positive gram-positive cocci in chains
Beta-hemolytic, bacitracin-sensitive, PYR-positive gram-positive cocci in chains
Alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive, bile-soluble gram-positive lancet-shaped diplococci
Catalase-positive, coagulase-positive gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters
approach: Name the trigger of rheumatic fever: Streptococcus pyogenes (group A) pharyngitis.
Recall its identifying tests: beta-hemolysis, bacitracin sensitivity, and PYR positivity.
Rule out the other streptococci and staphylococci by their own tests.
questions.why: Rheumatic fever follows pharyngitis caused by Streptococcus pyogenes, the group A streptococcus. In the lab it grows as gram-positive cocci in chains that are catalase negative, produce complete (beta) hemolysis on blood agar, are inhibited by bacitracin, and are PYR positive. Skin infections with group A strains can cause poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis but are not the classic trigger of rheumatic fever.
whyNot: This is Streptococcus agalactiae (group B), a cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis, not rheumatic fever.
Correct.
This is Streptococcus pneumoniae, which causes pneumonia, otitis media, and meningitis.
This is Staphylococcus aureus. It does not trigger rheumatic fever.

questions.stem: Which of the following sequences best explains his increased pulmonary artery pressure and right ventricular hypertrophy?
options: Chronic alveolar hypoxia from obstructive lung disease constricts and then remodels pulmonary arterioles
Recurrent thromboemboli from leg veins lodge in and gradually obstruct the pulmonary arteries
A left-to-right shunt delivers excess blood flow into the pulmonary circulation
High left atrial pressure backs up into the lungs, then pulmonary arterioles constrict and remodel
approach: Start upstream at the obstruction: mitral stenosis raises left atrial pressure.
Follow the pressure back: pulmonary veins, capillaries, and then pulmonary arteries.
Add the arterial response and its result: reactive constriction and remodeling raise the right ventricle's afterload, causing hypertrophy, a loud P2, and a parasternal heave.
questions.why: Mitral stenosis keeps left atrial pressure high. With no valves in the pulmonary veins, that pressure passes straight back to the pulmonary capillaries. The pulmonary arteries must then run at a higher pressure to keep blood moving forward, and over time the arterioles constrict and their walls thicken, raising pulmonary artery pressure further. The right ventricle faces this higher afterload and develops concentric hypertrophy, which produces the parasternal heave, while the loud P2 reflects forceful closure of the pulmonic valve.
whyNot: Hypoxic vasoconstriction from lung disease is a cause of pulmonary hypertension, but nothing in his case suggests chronic lung disease.
Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension needs a history of clots. His valve disease already explains the finding.
A shunt such as an atrial or ventricular septal defect causes pulmonary hypertension from excess flow. He has no shunt.
Correct.

topics: Pulmonary hypertension due to left heart disease

case: A 61-year-old woman is admitted to the hospital because of a 1-year history of episodic facial flushing, watery diarrhea, and wheezing, and more recent leg swelling and abdominal fullness. Imaging shows a small tumor in the terminal ileum and multiple liver metastases. Her 24-hour urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is 180 mg/24 h (reference about 2 to 9 mg/24 h). Physical examination shows jugular venous distention and a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Echocardiography shows thickened, retracted, poorly mobile tricuspid leaflets with severe tricuspid regurgitation, a thickened pulmonic valve, and normal mitral and aortic valves. Diagnosis: carcinoid heart disease from a metastatic ileal neuroendocrine tumor.

questions.stem: She also has a scaly rash on sun-exposed skin of her hands and neck and has become forgetful. Reduced synthesis of which cofactor best explains these new findings?
options: FAD and FMN, made from riboflavin
Tetrahydrobiopterin, made from guanosine triphosphate
NAD+ and NADP+, made in part from tryptophan
Thiamine pyrophosphate, made from thiamine
approach: Recognize the new findings as pellagra: dermatitis on sun-exposed skin, diarrhea, and dementia.
Link to the tumor: carcinoid cells convert a large share of dietary tryptophan into serotonin.
Recall that tryptophan is also a precursor for niacin, which forms NAD+ and NADP+.
questions.why: Tryptophan normally supplies part of the body's niacin, which is built into NAD+ and NADP+. A carcinoid tumor diverts a much larger share of tryptophan than normal into serotonin, so less is left for niacin synthesis. The result can be pellagra: dermatitis in sun-exposed areas, diarrhea, and dementia. Her diarrhea may come from both serotonin excess and pellagra.
whyNot: Riboflavin deficiency causes cheilosis, angular stomatitis, and glossitis. Riboflavin is not made from tryptophan.

Tetrahydrobiopterin is a cofactor for tryptophan hydroxylase, but it is made from GTP, and its deficiency causes a form of hyperphenylalaninemia with neurologic signs rather than a photosensitive rash.
Correct.
Thiamine deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, not a photosensitive dermatitis, and thiamine is not made from tryptophan.

questions.stem: An ileal carcinoid often causes no systemic symptoms until it has spread to the liver. Which venous route best explains why her symptoms appeared only after liver metastases formed?
options: Superior mesenteric vein draining into the portal vein
Inferior mesenteric vein draining into the splenic vein
Left gastric vein draining into the portal vein
Hepatic veins draining into the inferior vena cava
approach: Trace venous drainage of the ileum: superior mesenteric vein to portal vein to liver.
Recall that the liver inactivates serotonin (by monoamine oxidase) on this first pass.
Ask how liver metastases differ: they release products into the hepatic veins, which drain straight into the inferior vena cava and right heart.
questions.why: Blood from the ileum travels through the superior mesenteric and portal veins to the liver, which breaks down serotonin and other vasoactive products before they reach the systemic circulation. Liver metastases secrete these products downstream of that filter, into the hepatic veins, which empty directly into the inferior vena cava. The products reach the right heart in high concentration, causing flushing, diarrhea, bronchospasm, and right-sided valve damage. Primary tumors outside the portal drainage, such as bronchial or ovarian carcinoids, can cause the syndrome without liver spread.
whyNot: The ileum drains through the superior mesenteric vein into the portal vein, so serotonin from the primary tumor passes through the liver and is inactivated there.
The inferior mesenteric vein drains the distal colon and reaches the portal system through the splenic vein, so its blood also passes through the liver.
The left gastric vein drains the stomach into the portal vein, so its blood is filtered by the liver as well.
Correct.

questions.stem: A biopsy of the thickened tricuspid tissue would most likely show which of the following?
options: Surface plaques of smooth muscle cells in a mucopolysaccharide-rich matrix
Small, sterile fibrin-platelet vegetations along the lines of leaflet closure
Granulomas with plump macrophages, giant cells, and foci of fibrinoid necrosis
Ballooning leaflets with an expanded spongiosa and fragmented collagen fibers
approach: Recognize the lesion: right-sided valve thickening and retraction in a patient with carcinoid syndrome.
Recall that carcinoid plaques are fibrous deposits laid on top of the valve and endocardium.
Match the histology: smooth muscle cells and myofibroblasts in a matrix rich in mucopolysaccharides.
questions.why: Carcinoid heart disease produces plaque-like fibrous thickenings on the endocardium of the right heart chambers and on the tricuspid and pulmonic valves. They are made of smooth muscle cells and myofibroblasts in a matrix rich in acid mucopolysaccharides, laid on top of the existing valve. Serotonin and related products are thought to drive this fibrosis. The plaques stiffen and retract the leaflets, which typically causes tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis.
whyNot: Correct.
Small sterile vegetations describe nonbacterial thrombotic (marantic) endocarditis, seen with hypercoagulable states such as advanced cancer, mainly on left-sided valves.
Granulomas with activated macrophages (Anitschkow cells) and giant cells are Aschoff bodies of acute rheumatic carditis.
An expanded spongiosa in floppy leaflets describes myxomatous degeneration in mitral valve prolapse.

questions.stem: Her mitral and aortic valves are normal even though the tumor products are reaching her right heart in high amounts. Which enzyme and location best explain why the left-sided valves are spared?
options: Catechol-O-methyltransferase in the left atrial wall
Monoamine oxidase in the pulmonary vascular bed
Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase in the lung
Tryptophan hydroxylase in the alveolar epithelium
approach: Note the pattern: right-sided lesions with left-sided sparing.
Ask what lies between the right and left heart: the pulmonary circulation.
Recall that monoamine oxidase in the lung vascular bed breaks serotonin down to 5-HIAA before blood reaches the left heart.
questions.why: Blood from the right heart passes through the lungs before reaching the left heart. The pulmonary vascular bed takes up serotonin and breaks it down with monoamine oxidase to 5-HIAA, so much less reaches the mitral and aortic valves. Left-sided lesions do occur when this filter is bypassed, such as with a patent foramen ovale and right-to-left shunting, a primary bronchial carcinoid, or very high hormone levels.
whyNot: COMT mainly breaks down catecholamines such as epinephrine and dopamine, not serotonin, and the left atrial wall is not a major site of serotonin clearance.
Correct.
Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase makes serotonin from 5-hydroxytryptophan, so it would add serotonin rather than remove it.
Tryptophan hydroxylase is the rate-limiting enzyme for serotonin synthesis, so it would also add serotonin.

case: A 79-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after he lost consciousness while climbing two flights of stairs. For 6 months, he has had chest pressure and shortness of breath with exertion. Blood pressure is 118/84 mm Hg. A harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur is heard at the right upper sternal border and radiates to both carotid arteries. S2 is soft and single, and the carotid upstroke is weak and delayed. Echocardiography shows a three-cusp aortic valve with heavily calcified, poorly mobile cusps, an aortic valve area of 0.7 cm2 (reference about 3 to 4 cm2), a mean gradient of 48 mm Hg, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, and an ejection fraction of 60% (reference 55% to 70%). Serum calcium is 9.4 mg/dL (reference 8.5 to 10.2 mg/dL). Diagnosis: severe calcific aortic stenosis.

questions.stem: Which process best explains the calcium deposits in his aortic valve?
options: Metastatic calcification of normal tissue due to raised serum calcium and phosphate
Dystrophic calcification of damaged valve tissue despite normal serum calcium
Fibrous fusion of the commissures from earlier rheumatic valve inflammation
Myxomatous expansion of the spongiosa with proteoglycan accumulation
approach: Note the normal serum calcium.
Recall the two types of pathologic calcification: dystrophic (damaged tissue, normal calcium) and metastatic (normal tissue, high calcium).
Link to age-related wear on a three-cusp aortic valve: dystrophic.
questions.why: Calcific aortic stenosis of older adults results from years of mechanical stress and low-grade injury to the cusps, with lipid deposition, inflammation, and calcification that resembles bone formation. Because the calcium is laid down in damaged tissue while serum calcium is normal, it is dystrophic calcification. The calcium masses form in the cusps from the aortic side and stiffen them, typically without fusing the commissures.
whyNot: Metastatic calcification needs high serum calcium or phosphate, as in hyperparathyroidism or kidney failure. His calcium is normal.
Correct.
Rheumatic aortic stenosis shows commissural fusion and almost always involves the mitral valve too. His cusps are calcified with no mention of fusion or mitral disease.
Myxomatous change makes leaflets soft and floppy, causing prolapse and regurgitation rather than stenosis.

questions.stem: The cusps of the diseased valve developed from which of the following embryonic structures?
options: Endocardial cushion swellings of the truncus arteriosus
Atrioventricular endocardial cushions surrounding the atrioventricular canal
Septum primum tissue at the upper border of the primitive atrium
Mesenchyme of the right and left horns of the sinus venosus
approach: Identify the valve from the murmur: systolic ejection murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to the carotids means the aortic valve.
Recall that the aortic and pulmonic (semilunar) valves form in the outflow tract.
Pick the outflow tract cushions, which also receive neural crest cells.
questions.why: The aortic and pulmonic valves develop from endocardial cushion tissue in the outflow tract (truncal swellings), with a contribution from cardiac neural crest cells. As the outflow tract divides into the aorta and pulmonary trunk, small swellings on the cushions are hollowed out to form three cusps for each valve. Abnormal formation or fusion of these swellings produces a bicuspid aortic valve, which calcifies and becomes stenotic at a younger age than a three-cusp valve.
whyNot: Correct.
The atrioventricular cushions give rise to tissue of the mitral and tricuspid valves and the atrioventricular septum, not the semilunar valves.
The septum primum forms part of the interatrial septum and the flap of the foramen ovale.
The sinus venosus forms the smooth part of the right atrium, the coronary sinus, and part of the sinoatrial region.

questions.stem: Two days later, he develops atrial fibrillation. His shortness of breath worsens and his blood pressure falls abruptly. Which of the following best explains why loss of atrial contraction harms him more than it would harm a person with a normal heart?
options: Atrial fibrillation lengthens diastole and lets too much blood fill his thick ventricle
Losing the atrial contraction raises the gradient across his narrow aortic valve directly
Atrial fibrillation removes the main source of coronary blood flow to his thick ventricle
His stiff, thick ventricle relies on atrial contraction for a larger share of filling
approach: Identify the remodeling: aortic stenosis causes pressure overload and concentric hypertrophy.
Recall the cost: a thick, stiff ventricle relaxes and fills poorly in early diastole.
Apply it: atrial contraction supplies a larger share of filling, so its loss drops preload and stroke volume sharply.
questions.why: In a normal heart, most ventricular filling happens passively in early diastole, and atrial contraction adds a smaller share at the end. A concentrically hypertrophied ventricle from aortic stenosis is stiff and relaxes slowly, so passive filling falls and atrial contraction supplies a much larger part of the end-diastolic volume. When atrial fibrillation removes that contraction, and the fast rate also shortens diastole, preload and stroke volume drop. Pressure backs up into the lungs and cardiac output falls.
whyNot: Atrial fibrillation usually brings a fast ventricular rate, which shortens diastole and reduces filling, the opposite of this option.
The atrium sits upstream of the mitral valve. Losing its contraction lowers ventricular filling and stroke volume, so the aortic gradient tends to fall rather than rise.
Coronary flow is driven by aortic pressure during diastole. Atrial contraction does not supply coronary blood flow.
Correct.

questions.stem: Over the past year he has had recurrent melena from bleeding gastrointestinal angiodysplasia. He had no unusual bleeding earlier in life, including after a tooth extraction at age 60. Testing now shows loss of the largest von Willebrand factor (vWF) multimers. Which of the following mechanisms best explains this change?
options: Autoantibodies against ADAMTS13 block normal cleavage of the largest vWF multimers
Congestive liver injury reduces hepatic synthesis and secretion of vWF
High shear stress across the narrow valve unfolds vWF so ADAMTS13 cleaves it
A germline VWF mutation prevents normal assembly of multimers in endothelial cells
approach: Note the timing: no bleeding problems until recently, so the defect is acquired.
Link it to the valve: blood jets through a narrow aortic valve at high shear.
Recall that shear unfolds large vWF multimers and exposes the site cleaved by the protease ADAMTS13.
questions.why: Von Willebrand factor circulates as multimers, and the largest ones are the most effective at binding platelets to injured vessel walls. High shear stress across a stenotic aortic valve stretches these large multimers open and exposes the site that the plasma protease ADAMTS13 cleaves. The largest multimers are lost, which resembles type 2A von Willebrand disease. Together with bleeding from angiodysplasia this is called Heyde syndrome, and it often improves after the valve is replaced.
whyNot: Antibodies that block ADAMTS13 cause acquired thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, in which very large vWF multimers build up, the opposite of this finding.
vWF is made by endothelial cells and megakaryocytes, not the liver.
Correct.
An inherited defect usually causes bleeding from early life. His normal bleeding history until recently points to an acquired cause.

topics: Von Willebrand factor structure and function
